before.exam_tip_html: When writing about the Four Humours, link it to bigger themes: observation vs. religion, why ideas stayed the same for so long (Church support, no technology, respect for ancients), and how the Renaissance later challenged them. Examiners reward answers that show continuity and change.

Always discuss both sides of the boom. The examiner wants to see you understand it was not shared equally. Give specific examples and statistics for who benefited and who was left behind. Link the causes together — mass production cut prices, hire purchase made goods affordable, and advertising drove demand higher.

Link different types of terms together. For example, explain how losing the Saar and Upper Silesia directly made reparations harder to pay. Examiners reward answers that show how the Treaty’s terms interconnected, not just list them separately.

For questions about this period, discuss both continuity and change. Examiners want to see that you understand progress was not straightforward — old beliefs like miasma and the Four Humours persisted even as new ideas emerged. A balanced answer covering both sides will score higher marks.

Examiners want to see you understand both the legal and direct-action approaches. The NAACP won court cases (Brown v. Board), while the Montgomery Bus Boycott showed the power of mass protest. A top answer explains how these strategies worked together — legal victories gave moral authority, while direct action created the public pressure to enforce change. Remember to mention Emmett Till as a catalyst and the role of media in building support.

Do not dismiss appeasement as cowardly or stupid. Examiners reward answers that explain the context — WWI trauma, sympathy for German grievances, fear of communism, economic weakness, and no American support. Show you understand why it was followed before judging whether it was right. You can also mention the historian debate (Taylor vs Parker) for top marks.

When analysing why Stalin signed the Pact, show it was a logical if cynical choice. Explain how he was alienated at Munich, distrusted the guarantee to Poland, and needed time to rebuild the Red Army after the purges. Do not just call it “evil” — examiners reward answers that explain the reasoning behind decisions.

Questions often ask “how far” Kennedy and Johnson succeeded in reducing poverty. You need balance: acknowledge the achievements (poverty falling from 22% to 13%, Medicare, Head Start) but also explain the limits (25 million still in poverty, Vietnam diverting funds, conservative opposition, structural racism). Use specific statistics and named laws — the examiner rewards precise evidence. Compare Kennedy and Johnson: Kennedy set the vision but achieved little; Johnson passed the laws but was undone by Vietnam.

This is a classic “who was to blame?” essay topic. The exam question will name one cause and ask “How far do you agree?” — e.g. appeasement, Hitler’s foreign policy, the Nazi-Soviet Pact, or German remilitarisation. Start with that given factor, then add two more causes to show balance. Always reach a clear judgement in your conclusion — explain why one cause matters more than the others. Examiners reward answers that weigh causes against each other, not just list them.
